subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is the armament already provided for the destroyers built and in course of building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: For the destroyers already built armament was provided in Great Britain.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: And one was launched.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The Tribals built in Great Britain were provided with armament there, and of course the destroyers that we acquired from Great Britain were fully equipped when we got them.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But the one now building?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think some guns for the destroyer which is being built at Halifax are coming from Great Britain.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is the minister free to give the sizes and the number of the guns on these new Tribal boats which are being built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do lot know that I want to particularize in too much detail, but they run from 4-7 inch guns down to the Lewis and Bren guns.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The 4-7 inch guns-guns of that size-are built in Canada, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We are making some 4 inch guns. I am not sure about 4-7 inch guns, but I can find that out. The destroyers built in Great Britain are equipped with guns at the British yards there. I think 4-7 inch guns are also coming from Great Britain for the destroyers building in Halifax, but I am not quite sure on that point.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Would the minister care to make a statement as to the progress being made in the building of these Tribal destroyers? One was launched some months ago, and I understand that another is about ready to be launched. I would like to know, if the minister thinks it is all right to give the information, when the balance of the programme will be completed and when these destroyers will be in service. There are some misgivings as to the length of time required to build them and get them equipped and into actual service. We are all anxious to see this class of construction undertaken and carried out successfully in Canada. On the other hand, it is the feeling of everybody that the justification for building them is to have them fully equipped and ready for active service at the earliest possible date.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It is inevitable, I think, that the building of the first of these destroyers should take longer in this country than it would take in a country where more experience had been acquired in this type of work. It is inevitable that the building of the hull should take a little longer, and that there should be a delay in connection with the installation of the machinery, which is of a new type so far as this country is concerned, as compared with what might have been done in the yards of Great Britain and the United States, where long experience has been gained in that type of work. But, all things considered, I think progress is reasonably satisfactory. The destroyers will take somewhat longer to build and will cost a little more than if they had been constructed in Great Britain. On the whole, however, I think that if, as I said the other day, we are to have a navy in this country we should build in Canada as many ships for that navy as we possibly can, and we have to acquire experience in our own yards. Destroyers are vital constituent parts in any navy. I believe that in future years it will be said that, all things considered, we did wisely in undertaking the construction of these ships at the time we did. Further, when we formed our plans for the building of destroyers in Canada, there was continually in our minds the possibility that English yards would be bombed and that it might be difficult to carry on work there. Happily, in the last year or so that condition has pretty well passed away, and the British yards are doing their usual fine work. But in 1941, when we took this decision, there was a strong possibility that some of the British shipyards would find it very difficult indeed to carry on. So, that all in all, I think the decision was wise. While I should like to see the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
work proceed a little more rapidly, I understand the difficulties and delays, the labour problems and the problems connected with getting the machinery. Everything is being done, of course, that we can do from this end to speed up this work.	[DOT]

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I thank the minister for the answer he has given, but he has hardly answered my question as to the number included in this programme for the construction of Tribal destroyers, and when it is expected that the programme will be completed and each unit will be ready for service. One ship was launched some time ago and another one is nearly ready to be launched. It should be pretty well known by now when that will be equipped and ready for service. I should also like information with respect to the others.
The minister also admits that construction here costs more than it does in the older yards, in Great Britain and other places, and I appreciate that that is necessarily so. He informed the committee that the cost will be a little larger than in these older yards. I should like to know what he means by "a little."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Oh, well, I cannot give my hon. friend that information. As a matter of fact, I do not know how much more it will be. The destroyers are not yet completed. The work is being done on the first destroyer on the basis of cost plus a fixed fee. What the final cost will be I cannot tell my hon. friend at this moment. It is inevitable that it will be greater than in Great Britain. Our rates of labour are higher here than in Great Britain; our cost of material is somewhat higher. What the ultimate cost of that first destroyer will be I could not say at the moment. It will be greater-more than "a little". I am afraid it will be, substantially greater than it would be in Great Britain.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Fifty per cent more, may I ask the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
should think probably it would, on the first
destroyer.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But no more than 50 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Well, I do not know. It may be more.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Would the
minister care to give the committee the information as to the number of ships in the present programme, and when it is expected they will be completed, ready for active service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to the Tribal destroyers?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We already have four of these ships in commission.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But I mean the ones which are being built in the yards at Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The programme involves four ships there. We anticipate now that the last ship will be launched in May of next year. My hon. friend understands, of course, that when you have launched a ship of war you still have a great deal of work ahead of you. The installation of machinery, the trials of the ship, and all the rest are a problem in themselves just as great as, and in some cases perhaps greater than, the hull work. But it is anticipated now that the last destroyer will be launched in May, 1945.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not able to get the information from the minister; I will not press him if he informs the committee that it is not in the public interest to disclose it. The information I am asking for is, when will these ships be fully completed and equipped and ready for active service- the first of the programme of four Tribal destroyers, and the last of the four?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I should say to my hon. friend, although it can be only a guess, that the first ship, the one which has already been launched, the Micmac, will be commissioned next spring or early summer, a year or a little more than a year from now. The last one ought to be commissioned about a year after she is launched. She will be launched, we hope, next May; she should be commissioned in the following summer. I think we ought to make more rapid progress as we go along, and I should hope the last ship would be commissioned by the summer of 1946-not 1950, as someone suggested here the other day.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I recall very well the launching of the Micmac, the Tribal destroyer, in Halifax, at which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services was present, and Mrs. Macdonald, the wife of the minister, had the honour of christening that splendid ship, I also remember when the construction of destroyers in Canada was first mooted; there were many who thought it was impossible for Canada to undertake the building of this type of craft. But I recall travelling from Montreal to Halifax with a Mr. Mariner,

War Appropriation-Naval Services
who was connected with one of the Scottish shipbuilding concerns, and had been in Canada for a period of about a year or a year and one-half when the war broke out. He made the statement then that there was no reason why Canada should not be able to build its own destroyers. I was pleased, as I think was the country at large, when announcement was made by the navy department that this type of ship would be constructed in Canada.
I am surprised that the hon. member for Cumberland, with his knowledge of the difficulties experienced in his own town of Amherst with respect to aeroplane construction, would be critical of the time taken to bring to successful conclusion a new undertaking such as the one to which he referred. It is almost impossible in a country like Canada to build ships in the same time as in the shipyards of the old country. We did not have the facilities at the time, although the Halifax shipyards are well equipped now. We were without the skilled1 labour and material. It was not thought possible that the material would be available in this country. But all those obstacles were overcome and we were very happy on the occasion of the launching of the Micmac. I do not think it is a question of time, although we are all anxious to see those boats completed and launched at the earliest possible moment. What we should bear in mind is that Canadian workmen were able to build boats, something which we thought three years ago was impossible.
I think the Halifax shipyards have done exceptionally well in regard to the handling of those two contracts. One ship is afloat and! the other one is about to be launched. It is a matter of finishing up the fittings. I am looking forward to the day when we shall have not only those two in commission but many others built by Canadians in Canadian shipyards.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I commended this policy and the minister for having undertaken the construction of those ships in Canada and in Nova Scotia. This is in line with the policy that was proposed by other governments in previous years, although unfortunately not carried out. I recognize also that it is to be expected that the initial ships would take longer to build, than they have in other yards. On the other hand, I think it is perfectly proper, in seeking information covering this enormous expenditure for a very worthy purpose, to ask for information as to the time it takes to build those vital ships and as to the cost and the justification for the additional cost. If this
committee is not to get that information we might as well adjourn. We are here for the purpose of getting information.
I do not wish to press the minister unduly, but I should have liked to have from him a statement as to whether he considers that the construction programme, has proceeded with the expedition that we should reasonably expect to be the case in a time of war and at a time when we are in desperate need1 of having those ships commissioned for active service, I am not critical of the programme, 'but I do want information as to the cost in Canada in comparison with the cost elsewhere, I want information as to the time it takes to build those ships in this country as compared with the time taken in other countries. I am glad this programme has been undertaken. I regret it was not undertaken by the government much earlier. I hope that it will be a success and that it will be an established programme in the years that lie ahead, although we all recognize that the building of ships of war after the successful termination of the war will be extremely limited in comparison with the needs at the present time.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
understand that there is some trouble on the diesel-powered ships in regard to seawater getting into the oil tanks. Has the water been allowed to get in after the oil is on the ship or when it is being loaded, or is it oil that comes up from South America?

Mr. MacNICOJii: This item refers to fuel for ships. Where is the item that refers to fuel for the heating of the barracks and the yards?

10.	Acquisition, construction, charter, repair and upkeep of ships, $82,282,000.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I observe that the total estimate of the department has been reduced by approximately $79,000,000. This particular item has been reduced by about $85,000,000, as against a reduction of $79,000,000 on the total estimate for this department. From that I would take it that the department is under the impression that the shipbuilding programme is reaching its objective. I should like to ask if that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend is using the figure of $167,000,000, which was the estimated expenditure for the present year. I may tell him, however, that we did not spend that sum. The year is not quite over yet and consequently I have not the exact figure, but I should think it would be somewhat less than the figure of 8167,000,000. It is true, as my hon. friend points out, that the estimate for this year is considerably less, but we are still building a good many ships in this country. As I indicated in my statement the other day, we propose to add a very considerable number of ships to the navy during the present year, so that our shipbuilding programme is by no means completed.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Could the minister give us the kind of ships that have been built during the past year, and what kind of craft are being built now, such as landing craft, seeps and small craft of that kind? This item deals with acquisition, construction and charter. How many has the department bought; how many has it constructed and how many has it chartered during the past year, with the cost in each case if that can be given?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: To mention some of the ships we are building there are destroyers, frigates, corvettes-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Could the minister give the number of each?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Well, if I did so, it would have to be very approximate: destroyers, frigates, corvettes, Algerine mine-sweepers, Bangor mine-sweepers, Bassett mine-sweepers, wooden mine-sweepers of 105 feet and 126 feet; some motor launches, which means Fairmiles; some patrol vessels and various types of auxiliary vessels such as harbour vessels, gate vessfcls, examination vessels and so on. That would be a rough description of the ships we are building.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What about landing craft and seeps?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, not for our navy.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How is this item of $82,000,000 divided or broken down under these four headings? What is the amount of each?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Acquisition and construction would be about $47,000,000; charters would be about $1,000,000; the repair and upkeep of ships would be about $33,000,000, all in round figures, making a total of $82,000,000.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There would appear to be a misleading article in the copy of the Toronto Star Weekly I have in my hand, if the government is not buying craft of this kind. This article refers to amphibious jeeps, amphibious ducks, and seeps.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Of course some craft are being built in this country, but not for the Canadian navy; probably that is what the article refers to.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Then who would have control of these; the army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Some ships of that kind are being used by the army and some are being built for Great Britain.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
There are many types of ships being built in this country for Great Britain. I am speaking now of ships being built for the Canadian navy, and none of those landing craft are for the navy.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is there a plan on foot to build any of them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Then, if there is an invasion of Europe by the allies, Canadians will have to ride in the landing craft of other nations; is that true? They will have to be carried in the craft of other countries; the Canadian navy will not carry them; it will be other allied countries which will supply the boats?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There is nothing unusual about that. We are using guns which were produced in other countries, while some other countries are using guns made here. We might be using the ships of another country and at the same time be building ships here for Great Britain and the United States. There is nothing abnormal or unusual about that. Certain craft of that type have been built in Canada, but I say that none has been built for the Canadian navy. I believe the Canadian army had some, and perhaps some were built in this country for the United Kingdom, while of course a great many were built in the United States and some are built in England. We are not building any in this country for the Canadian navy as such.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In
case of an emergency, if Canada needed some of these craft in a hurry, she would have to go to other allied countries to get them; is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know that my hon. friend should put it in that way. I do not think hon. gentlemen should always try to put the worst possible construction on everything.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not mean it in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Then I will say, Mr. Chairman, that it sounds very much like it; that we will have to go to somebody else, virtually with our hat in our hands, saying, " Please give us ships." I do not think this country has to apologize for what it has done in the matter of providing ships, guns or anything else. It is a common thing for one country to undertake a certain line of work and give its surplus to another country. We have built a hundred ships here for Great Britain. We have built a few ships for the United States. We do not say, because of that, 100-101 -
that the British navy is falling to pieces, or that England has to come begging us for ships. We were able to help Britain in the case of ships, and we were able to do so in connection with guns, ammunition and depth charges. We Were able to give some of these to other countries, and they were glad to accept them. In return we took some things from those other countries. It is an exchange that is honourable, reasonable and fair on all sides. As to landing craft, we have not built any for the Canadian navy, but such craft have been built in the country and I have no doubt that there will be a sufficient number of those craft to deal with the situation when it arises.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am just as proud of the Canadian navy as the minister is, and I was not casting any reflection upon it or upon the building programme. But I know how the boys feel; they like to be carried in their own Canadian boats, and that was why I rose and said what I did. I make no apology for doing so, and I know the minister understands how I feel about the matter.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: In the case of boats that are chartered, what is the relation of the minister's department to the Department of Transport? To what extent is the Department of Transport involved in the charter of these boats; on what basis is the charter hire decided, and by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The director of marine services, who is an official of the Department of Transport, acts as our agent in this matter. With respect to the basis upon which boats are chartered, there is at the coast a committee known as an advisory board, which examines the vessel and determines what it thinks a fair charter would be. I believe that the committee on the east coast consists of three, and that there is on the west coast a similar committee which carries out those duties. They work pretty well along certain formulae; they look at the ship, allowing so much for depreciation, so much for administration expenses and the like. Then they fix what they regard as a fair charter to pay for that ship.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
We understand, of course,
that the navy is operating in the Mediterranean, and in all the seven seas. Do those ships come back to Canada for repairs, or are they repaired in the ports of the different united nations? If they return to Canada, what places in this country are being used for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Some of the ships would be repaired here, and some



War Appropriation-Naval Services
might be repaired in Great Britain or elsewhere. I should assume that if ships were in the Mediterranean area they might be repaired there. Others might be repaired1 in the United States. In this country, starting at Newfoundland, the repair yards would be at St. John's, and at Bay Bulls one is under construction. There are several places in Nova Scotia where repairs can be made. Then, there is, of course, the Saint John dry dock at Saint John, New Brunswick, where repairs might be carried out. In the summer months repairs can be done at Quebec and Montreal. On the west coast repairs can be undertaken at Vancouver or Victoria.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The policy is to make
repairs at the most convenient point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It
has to be done in that way, yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The people of Stettler,

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Some weeks ago I asked the minister to check up on a small boat which had been requisitioned and then returned to the owner. Has he had time to gather any information?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I have before me a return, sessional paper 253, which was brought down for another member in April, 1942. From a study of these papers I have come to the conclusion that in these matters there is anything but cooperation between the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. There is certainly an undue amount of red tape which causes inconvenience to citizens whose properties have been requisitioned.
For instance, I find that this particular boat was taken over by the naval department on December 7. The Department of Transport had the boat inspected on December 9 by a marine surveyor, and then on December 13 by a steamship inspector, at which time a valuation was placed on the boat. On January 3, after a considerable length of time, the advisory board, to which the minister referred, placed on the boat a valuation which was incidentally less than that of the marine inspector. This report was not sent to the naval department by the Department of Transport until September 21; seven months passed before the findings of this board were reported to the minister's department. The result was that this citizen whose boat had been chartered had to wait seven months for his first cheque, and he received this only after making a special trip to Ottawa.
As another illustration of the lack of cooperation, this citizen was notified on September 9, by the engineer in charge of Halifax harbour, working under the minister's department, that the charter was to be cancelled or that the department desired to cancel the charter which had been entered into, and the citizen was requested to come and get his boat. On October 18, nearly six weeks later, the Department of Transport executed a new charter with the citizen.
There are a couple of other points I should like to call to the minister's attention. The marine inspector of the Department of Transport valued this boat at $16,500, but the board, to which the minister has referred, reduced this valuation by twenty-five per cent to 513,200, on the ground that the surveyor had allowed a twenty-five per cent war appreciation over the actual value of the boat.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
I assume that the minister's department is responsible for the examination of boats placed in dry dock. This boat was placed in a dry dock the latter part of February, 1941, and was there for fourteen days. The evidence here shows that ceiling planks were removed; conditions were found to be good, and so forth. As a result of this examination a requisition was made for the expenditure of S844 on the boat, and apparently this was i approved and spent toward the end of February on an annual overhaul. On April 8, after the boat had been in dry dock for two weeks and had been given this outfitting costing SS44, she comes back into dry dock again for two days to get a coat of paint. Then a month later she comes back into dry dock again for another coat of paint. There is no evidence in the return to show what these two extra coats of paint cost. The interesting part is that a few weeks after these expenditures on the boat the minister's own engineers discovered that the boat was rotten and would require approximately $5,000 to make it seaworthy. On the strength of that they notified the owner to take his boat back.
The confusing situation is that two inspectors of the transport department set an appraisal value on the boat of $16,500, and then $13,200; that the minister's own engineers considered the boat worth overhauling to the tune of $1,000 of the ratepayers' money, and then a couple of weeks later they discover that the boat is rotten and unfit for service. When the owner was asked to take the boat back, there is a copy of a telegram here in which he offered the department the free loan of the boat for the rest of the season, and the department replies that the boat simply cannot be used at all. Somebody in one or other of those departments is grossly inefficient and wasteful of the public's money. If you are going to put a boat that is rotten, that cannot be used, that must be discarded, into dry dock and spend nearly a thousand dollars on it-and incidentally there was another five hundred dollars of the taxpayers' money spent before the boat was returned-I should like to know who is at fault, who does not know his job. I think the taxpayer has a right to know why we should spend one thousand or fifteen hundred dollars on a boat which two weeks later is declared to be rotten.

Mr. Chairman, I might be allowed now to put on Hansard answers to certain questions which were asked during the course of the discussion on these estimates. The hon. member for Vancouver South asked a question about the defence of the Pacific coast and the fishermen's reserve. I may tell him that the fishermen's reserve is being disbanded as a reserve. Instructions to that effect have been issued. Members of the reserve are now given the opportunity of joining either the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve or the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve or of returning to their pursuit of fishing. The fishermen's reserve was organized before the war, I think in 1937 or 1938, for, as I understand, one particular purpose, and that was based on the knowledge which these men had of the coast. They were to serve in their own boats on the west coast. Later I think that term of service was extended to apply to service anywhere in their own boats. The main purpose for which they were organized they have discharged and discharged, I believe, very satisfactorily. They had charge of rounding up the Japanese fishing boats on the British Columbia coast, and they did that, I believe, very successfully, taking into their charge in all some one thousand boats. The situation is different now from what it was in the early days of the war. The menace from Japanese boats on that coast has disappeared. The boats have all been taken. We ourselves have a stronger naval force there than we had in the beginning. In all the circumstances it was felt that the fishermen's reserve might be disbanded, and1 that has been done.
I should like to say a word of appreciation to these men for what they did and how effectively and loyally they carried out their duties. I understand that some of the fishermen's reserve craft are being returned to their owners, but approximately thirty boats are being retained by the navy, and most of them will be employed on patrol work.

speechtext: Why could these fishermen not revert to the same status; in other words, why could we not have a fishermen's reserve? There is not one on the Atlantic coast, I know. But on the west coast they would serve a very useful purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As I have intimated, the great purpose-I am given to understand so by the personnel officers of my department-in forming the fishermen's reserve was that which they have already carried out. My hon. friend will understand that their boats are small. . They are fishing boats. They are really not combat boats but they are very useful for patrol purposes. These men know the British Columbia coast. They were able, consequently, to seize many of those Japanese boats which were on the coast at the outbreak of war with Japan. I believe that was one of the greatest purposes in having them formed, to deal with any danger which might arise from the outbreak of war with Japan. They discharged that duty. They did seize a thousand Japanese boats, acquired them, rounded them up.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That was all done in a few days.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I know, but if these men had not been there some of those boats might have been prowling around for months. The fishermen's reserve knew where to go to get the boats and they got them. The danger from Japanese coastal boats operating to-day has now disappeared through the efforts of these men.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It disappeared right after Japan struck.	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes, it disappeared, and therefore the need for continuing the reserve did not appear to the officers of the department to be as great as it used to be, and the course which I have outlined was decided upon and is now being carried out. The terms of their enlistment were limited. At first the terms were that they would be used only on the west coast and only in their own boats. That was later extended to a provision that they would go anywhere, provided they went in their own boats. That is not full active service as we understand it in the navy. Consequently it was considered better at this time to make a clear demarcation and say to them "If you wish to go fishing, you may do so Fishing
[Mr. Green.J
is a very important industry, and you may return to it; or if you prefer you may remain in the navy." That is the choice we have given them, and they are now acting according to their own desires.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I would ask the minister to give some further consideration to the whole question. On the Pacific coast the army has units known as the Pacific coast militia rangers, whose work is really reconnaissance the same as the work of the fishermen. The rangers are still carrying on, and doing very good) work; and I think some similar scheme could be worked out for the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
shall be very glad to consider that.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I think a little more should be said on behalf of the fishermen's reserve, in support of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South. I would say that the fishermen's reserve did much more work on the Pacific coast than merely taking in the Japanese boats.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Very much more.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is all very well to look at the situation now, but remember what we were faced with in 1939, 1940 and 1941. No one knew what the Japanese would do, and these fishermen performed a splendid service. I believe more should be said about them. I will say this to the minister. I have discussed this matter with men in the fishermen's reserve, and they say, "There is no use in our attempting to go into the navy, because we have not been to college. If we do join the navy we are looked down upon by the naval man who has been at college." But they add, "We can take any of the boats and go into any bay in British Columbia, or take it to any town or village on the coast, which these men who have been to college cannot do." Most of the men to whom I have spoken say that there is no use in their going into the navy, and they are going back into industrial life. I rose particularly to tell the minister that these men served a much more useful purpose than merely seizing the Japanese boats. Now these men have been discarded, and I should like to know if they will get any consideration in connection with the granting of pensions. We considered these men extremely valuable two years ago, and we do not know when they may be needed again, because we have very little in the way of a navy on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My hon. friend must realize that one cannot defend a coast with fishing boats.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
We do not intend to.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Then what is the point? The fishermen's reserve performed a very useful service in capturing these Japanese boats and in reconnoitering the bays and harbours along the British Columbia coast; but to say that any such reserve is capable of dealing with anything in the nature of an attack is simply to lose all sense of proportion. They cannot do it, and it was never contemplated that they should do it. It was contemplated that they would do certain reconnaissance work and take over the Japanese fishing boats should any trouble arise with Japan, as trouble did arise; and they performed a very useful and valuable function. As to these men saying that they have no chance in the navy because they are not college men, I cannot understand that attitude. To-day in the Royal Canadian Navy there are a thousand officers from the naval reserve; that is, from the merchant service. How many of those were college men? Very few, I should think; they are practical seamen, but they are holding various positions in the navy from skipper to skipper-lieutenant, to lieutenant, up to lieutenant commander and commander, and some of them have the rank of captain. These men are in very much the same position as members of the fishermen's reserve; they are practical seamen, and one thousand of them have obtained commissioned rank. So that I think it is unfair to assume that because a man does not have a college education he cannot get anywhere in the navy.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How many from the fishermen's reserve have joined the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend that figure.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Many hon. members have already paid tribute in glowing terms to the minister, the officers and men of the Royal Canadian Navy and the officials of the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. I have in mind particularly the contribution that has been made by hon. members from Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg referred to the splendid facilities at Deep Brook, if not the largest, one of the largest, training centres in the British empire. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare referred to the naval repair facilities, and expressed the hope that in the post-war period these shipyard facilities would continue to operate as they are doing at the present time. Then my colleague from Halifax referred to our city, dealing more particularly with housing and other related conditions ap applied to the naval service. I should like to support the remarks of my colleague from Halifax, and ask the minister to give these matters his most favourable attention. Having been premier of Nova Scotia for many years, the minister is familiar with conditions not only in the city of Halifax but throughout the province. He knows it is necessary to prepare post-war plans that will keep Nova Scotia in its present favourable position, if we are to satisfy the fishermen and other elements in that province. A great many men of Nova Scotia have entered the naval service; in fact it is well known that there has always been a waiting list of men desiring to join the navy, particularly from the fishing districts, where the young men are very anxious to take part in the activities of the naval service.
My colleague made a very strong case on behalf of the port of Halifax. We all remember that in the last war Halifax played a very important part in connection with the handling of munitions, the assembling of convoys and the transportation of troops from Canada to England, and it has played an equally important part in this war. Our thought in Nova Scotia, and perhaps more particularly in Halifax, has been expressed by the hon. member for Cumberland; that is, we do not want to be forgotten when the war is over. We want Halifax to continue to be the main artery for goods entering and leaving Canada from and to overseas. We believe the eastern ports should be used to their full capacity in connection with overseas trade. In the past we have seen shipments of grain, cattle and other supplies sent through United States ports because it is alleged that the shorter rail haul to those ports makes it more economical to ship that way. I trust that the minister, with his knowledge of the requirements of Nova Scotia, realizing the important part that Halifax has played in the war effort, will not permit that condition to exist following this war, when victory will have crowned the efforts of the united nations.
I should like to endorse the very fine tributes that have been paid to the activities of the Royal Canadian Navy. I do not propose at this late hour to make any extended remarks in that connection, but there are one or two items I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. While we in Nova Scotia, each and every one of us, as has been stated by other hon. members, place the winning of the war as first and foremost in our thoughts, we do feel that members of this committee should give some thought to post-war plans. We consider that these plans are necessary in the far east coast perhaps to a greater extent

War Appropriation-Naval Services
than in central Canada. There are in this section of Canada industrial activities which will carry on for many years, probably for fifteen or twenty or more years, but we in the extreme east-and I believe the same applies to the extreme west-have not enjoyed that development to the same extent. I say we must make plans which will include all parts of Canada and more particularly have I in mind my native province of Nova Scotia.
No one can say how soon or how suddenly this war may end. It is anyone's guess as to just how long or how brief a time may pass before victory will be ours. No one can foretell. But one thing is sure, namely, that we cannot begin too early to plan for the post-war period. Long before the ink is dry on the peace treaty we must be ready to deal with the problems of peace. It is because of that I place before the minister the necessity of carrying on shipbuilding, and more particularly ship repairing in Nova Scotia.
My main thought in rising to take part in the debate is to deal with activities which will come directly under the item before the committee. I refer to the work carried' on by the smaller craft. Other hon. members have spoken about the great work of the destroyers and the corvettes. I have in mind particularly the work being done at the port of Halifax and along the shore by smaller craft such as auxiliary vessels, armed yachts, Fairmiles and1 mine-sweepers.
I pause to speak about mine-sweepers. If any hon. member were to visit the city of Halifax or the town of Dartmouth early in the morning at any time of the year, perhaps as early as five o'clock, and in any kind of weather-possibly a stormy winter morning- he would see mine-sweepers nosing out toward the head of the harbour. There the minesweepers clear the path for the convoys. The minister outlined1 in detail what took place off the head of Halifax harbour last June when a large number of mines-I do not care to mention the number, because the minister did not do so-were sown in the path of the outgoing ships. It is this type of work, carried on by the men who serve on these mine-sweepers, that has made possible for us the shipping overseas of great cargoes with a minimum of loss, so that our men over there may be fed, so that supplies may go to England, and munitions be supplied to our troops, who are helping to fight the battle for freedom.
Therefore I say that Halifax, and the men who serve in that port, have played1 a very important part in this war. I pay my tribute to those men who daily face hardships in their task of keeping clear and making safe the passage to and from the port of Halifax.

I hold in my hand1 a booklet in which appear views of Halifax harbour, depicting more particularly some of the large ships which sail into that port, unassisted, without the use of tugs. To illustrate that, one need1 only think of the Empress of Britain, a ship of 42,348 tons, sailing in, without tugs towing her, as it did in June, 1939, when carrying the King and Queen. She made a complete turn in our harbour and sailed out to sea. Remembering that, hon. members will have some idea of the type of harbour we have in the extreme east at the Atlantic coast port of Halifax.
I listened with interest and attention to the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, tell us about the harbours on the Pacific coast. I do not wish to make any attempt to detract from Vancouver harbour, or any other harbour on the west coast; but I do point out that at Halifax we have one of the grandest, finest and most natural harbours in the world to-day.
I refer now to the second picture in this booklet, showing three large liners.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What about Saint John.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What about Saint John? I
hesitate to make a comparison betwen Saint John and Halifax. One who knows the real facts seldom does. I am reminded of a story I heard some years ago about a number of visitors who were spending some time in Saint John-and I hope the hon. member for Royal will not take exception to the story. These visitors who were in Saint John one evening were wondering what they might do to fill in an hour's time. One of them had a bright idea, and said, " Let us go down, wait around and see the tide come in." We have no tides in Halifax harbour, so that we do not have to wait for them. We have no ice there in the winter. It is a port which can be used 365 days in the year. Ships sail in at all times, without the least trouble so far as tides are concerned. Not a single dollar has been spent on dredging in that port as long as I can remember-and I am getting up in years. To my knowledge, for at least thirty-five or forty years, not one dollar has been spent for that reason. So that the excellence of our harbour, for the use not only of our own Royal Canadian Navy, but of those of allied nations, must be apparent to all.
May I refer again to the service being rendered by the men who sail on small craft. The night of Wednesday, February 24, was exceptionally stormy at Halifax. Eighteen inches of snow fell that night, and the velocity of the wind was said to be fifty miles an hour. Had any of you hon. gentlemen been at

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Halifax on that night, with your coat collars turned up, your gloves on, wearing your overshoes, and with your hat pulled down over your ears, you would have still felt the effect of the wind. I wonder if you can visualize these small craft sent out that night to carry on patrol work. Would the minister give this matter some thought? Would he consider whether it is necessary to send out the small Fairmile craft on such stormy nights? I realize fully that the work must be done, but I am just a little concerned as to whether it is altogether necessary to send out these small boats on nights such as I have described.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because of a front-page article which appeared in one of the Halifax papers at that time. Quite naturally the article states:
Six tiny Fairmile launches push their sleek noses into the teeth of the worst maritime blizzard in years, February 24, on sudden orders to supply patrol protection, presumably for a convoy.
There is another type of man in whom I am interested, the man who is wounded or who, because of the type of service he has rendered, is not able to continue in active duty. I do not desire to take up much time in discussing this matter. When I was in Halifax a short time ago I visited the military hospital. I saw one man who had been returned from overseas with twelve wounds in his arms and head. I saw another Halifax man who, I regret to say, is not likely ever to leave that hospital. Many of these men require rest, and it is to them I direct the attention of the minister. A man may have served his country well overseas, or in the navy on shore patrol or on the high seas. At times he requires rest, and I suggest to the minister that there should be a rest or convalescent home in Nova Scotia situated close to Halifax where these men could regain their health in order to be able once more to take up their dangerous tasks. I have no particular place in mind and I know the minister is familiar with the beauty spots along our rugged shore. There are a number of places, such as beautiful St. Margaret or Queensland or Hubbard or many other such places. Any one of those would be an ideal place in which to locate a rest home such as I have in mind. Not only would such a home serve the navy, but it could be used to bring others back to a normal state of health. When you have something good to sell, you have a fairly easy task; when you have something nice to talk about, you can go on for any length of time, but I shall not say anything further about the port of Halifax. I do hope the minister will give consideration to this suggestion of having a convalescent home close to the naval base of Halifax.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I should like to say just a word on this matter. It was my intention .to make some complimentary references to the port of Halifax. The senior hon. member for Halifax has said quite a bit about that port, and since the rules of the house will not permit needless repetition there is perhaps nothing more I can say on that subject at this time. The eloquent and informative address made by the minister when introducing his estimates outlined an amazing achievement. The lucid outline of the growth of our navy, the wonderful service it has performed in this global war and the bravery of our boys who man our ships is a story that should incite pardonable pride in the hearts of all Canadians. It is only another instance of what a resourceful country with a patriotic people can achieve in cooperation with a ministry well manned, well planned and possessing the wisdom to select the executive and key men capable of initiating, developing and bringing to a successful conclusion the most amazing job that has been done by our navy.
I am sure we were all pleased and encouraged with the prospectus of the future submitted by the minister. I think from what he said we can hope that our navy will be maintained at sufficient strength to keep our sea lanes open and to protect and give freedom of the seas to our merchant marine which we expect to be plying the seven seas, carrying to other countries those commodities which they need and which they cannot produce and returning to Canada laden with the products of those countries. If it is the hope of our government that our navy is to be kept to that strength; if our merchant marine is to be maintained, then may we hope that the means of repairing and rebuilding these ships will also be maintained. When the time of peace comes and when rehabilitation is taking place in every phase of the life of this country, if shipyards are found to be necessary; if naval bases are found to be necessary, we hope that they will be maintained in the locations they now occupy and that we shall not be subjected to a programme of centralization which would destroy rather than enhance our prospects so far as our commercial life is concerned.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am not rising to extol the virtues of Esquimalt harbour; I rise to pay a just compliment to the fishermen's reserve and the Vancouver island motor-boat squadron which served us so faithfully in British Columbia, particularly on Vancouver island, at a time when we were a little nervous as to what was going to happen. After December, 1942, the Japs began to come closer to our Canadian shores by way of the Aleutian islands.
ie04

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Many of us were concerned about how far they would come and we were anxious to get all the protection possible, not only from the fishermen in that part of British Columbia but also from the Vancouver island motorboat squadron. The latter were serving entirely voluntarily. They were prepared to move troops at any time from one part of the island to the other or to evacuate the citizens of the island should that become necessary. I do not think that I as the member for Victoria, B.C., and speaking also for 'he district of Nanaimo-Captain Chambers s on duty-should let this occasion pass without saying "Thank you" to these people.
Further, I should like publicly to thank the private owners of motor-boats in Seattle. They invited a committee from Vancouver and Victoria to confer with a similar committee in Seattle to discuss the possibility of evacuating the citizens of Vancouver island. At the conclusion of a short meeting they offered to look after all the people on the southern end of the island, leaving the responsibility of the evacuation of the northern end to the Vancouver island motor-boat squadron. I think now is the time, Mr. Chairman, that we should recognize that service.
If the minister feels that the time has come when he can dispense with the services of the fishermen, I think they, too, should be duly thanked. We are, of course, delighted that the building of boats has progressed to such a point that the minister can afford to do that and that the fortunes of war have so changed that the danger is not now so apparent as it was then. I rise on this occasion to thank those three classes of people, the fishermen, the Vancouver island motor-boat squadron, ind the private owners of motor-boats in Seattle and northern Washington.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to make any extended remarks, but f must say I was surprised that the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) went out of lis way a few moments ago to abuse the port of Saint John, New Brunswick. I am sorry that the hon. member who represents Saint John is not here to-night because of illness. I am quite sure that he would have taken up the cudgels on behalf of his native city had he been here.
When I was speaking the other night I mentioned the fact that the ports of Saint John and Halifax should not be forgotten after the war is over. No one recognizes more clearly than I what a splendid asset this country has in the great port of Halifax, but I also recognize, as I am sure do the people of Canada, we have also a splendid port in TMr. Mayhew.]
Saint John, which is to-day and has been for a great many years, one of the great winter ports of this country, and whose worth to the Dominion of Canada cannot be overestimated. In the city of Saint John, as the minister mentioned to-day, we have one of the largest dry docks in existence in the British empire; as a matter of fact, I think it was the largest dry dock in the empire until just a few years ago. In that dry dock during this war a great many naval vessels and a great many merchant ships have been repaired.
I just wanted to take this opportunity, as one who lives in the province of New Brunswick and close to the port of Saint John, to say that we are very proud indeed of the port of Saint John, and also to express the opinion that the Dominion of Canada as a whole owes a great debt to this port, as I think all Canadians whether they come from Halifax or any other part of this country should recognize freely and fully.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I should like to say, as one coming from the maritime province of Manitoba, that we have been forgotten in that capacity. I wish to join this testimonial meeting to-night with respect to the merits and possibilities for after-the-war development of various parts of this country, to draw again to the attention of the government and of this House of Commons the too often forgotten port of Churchill. Those of us who live in the west and fought for a considerable period of time to have that port established have viewed with some disquietude its almost complete lack of use and the complete lack of consideration for it during the war period, and I am now just giving notice that in the days to come, when our thoughts will be turned more to the internal development of Canada than they are to-day, more will be heard of the port of Churchill and the maritime province of Manitoba.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I was very glad to hear the hon. members representing Saint John and Halifax speak on behalf of those great ports, and I quite agree with what they said. I think, however, when they were speaking of these great ports, they should have given thanks and praise to the women of the women's naval auxiliaries of Canada for supplying the men who go out on ships from these ports with warm clothing and many other comforts. I think these women deserve a great deal of credit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Before we proceed with this item perhaps I

War Appropriation-Naval Services
might give the answers to questions that have been asked by various members. To answer, first, questions that were asked with regard to the medical side of the naval service, the figure of 4-9 doctors per thousand personnel which was referred to includes forty doctors who were serving with the British navy and who took no part whatever in caring for Royal Canadian Navy personnel. If you excluded that figure, and it should properly be excluded, the number of medical officers in the Royal Canadian Navy would be four per thousand.
I was also asked how many ships carry medical officers. The number of our ships carrying medical officers is forty-seven.
I was also asked what happened on ships that had no medical officer aboard. In that case, ships of the corvette class, which do not ordinarily carry a medical officer, carry a sick-berth rating. These are ratings specially trained in first aid and the treatment of minor illnesses. Many of them are graduate male nurses. Ships of still smaller types such as motor torpedo-boats and Fairmiles and similar craft usually operate from a base or depot ship where adequate medical facilities exist, so that the need of having somebody skilled in medicine aboard is not so great. In escort or convoy work there is always one and there are usually two medical officers in each group of escort ships, whose services are available to any ship in the group. In addition, ten per cent of the crews of all ships have had instruction in first aid.
I was asked by the hon. member for Yale what steps had been taken to control venereal disease. At the larger bases, venereal disease control officers have been appointed, whose duty it is to check the ravages and the spread of this disease. There is also a veneral disease control officer at naval service headquarters. All medical officers and all commanding officers have been advised as to the most effective measures which can be taken to control the disease. All naval personnel are given lectures from time to time, beginning as soon as they enter the service, on how this disease can be avoided.
My hon. friend the member for Cumberland asked about night vision. I am able to tell him that facilities for testing night vision are available at Cornwallis, at Halifax, Esquimalt and at St. John's, Newfoundland. The majority of officers and ratings of the seaman and signal branch have been tested for night vision, and the testing is still going on as rapidly as conditions permit.
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked as to the number of civilian personnel in Newfoundland. On January 31 of this year
we had 253 civilian personnel in Newfoundland. I do not include in that figure hourly-paid workers but just civil servants properly so-called, and they numbered 253.
I was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South something about the training at Cornwallis and Kings. I was asked to endeavour to find out what the exact percentage of failures was. I think somebody suggested that I take the last ten classes. I have here the total number of naval personnel who were officer candidates at Cornwallis during the period from August 10 to February 8 last. I find that the number of failures is just under thirty-three per cent. That is the number over that period of seven months.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Was there any month when the failures were extremely high?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The numbers vary. Usually these men come up every week before the selection board, and the number who appear before the board varies. Sometimes it is as low as nine; at other times as many as twenty-seven appear in one week, and the number of failures consequently varies. Some weeks it has been two; some weeks, 12; some weeks, four; other weeks, nine, and so on. What particular week had my hon. friend in mind?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
believe that last night the month of December was mentioned. It was either the latter part of November or the first part of December when, according to these boys, so many of them failed.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

speechtext: Sixty per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

That may be the particular week, but it is difficult to draw any general conclusions from the figures for one week. I think the best test would be to take the whole period of the operation of the school at Cornwallis, for which, as I say, the number of failures is just about thirty-three per cent.

speechtext: I think the reason why these boys brought the matter up is that, on the examination before they tried, there had been very few failures, and then in their week practically all failed.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

As I say, it varies from time to time. That is the general story so far as Cornwallis is concerned.
I was asked something about the depth of the water at the end of the wharf at Cornwallis. I have not been there for some time, but I am informed that it varies from six to ten feet at the head of the wharf at low water. The hon. member for Yale wanted to know about the sea cadet camp at Comox. I understand that that camp will not be used in the coming summer, and that instead, a camp at a place called Whiteclilf park, some fifteen miles from Vancouver, will be used by the sea cadets of British Columbia.

speechtext: Where is that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Whitecliff park is near Vancouver. I am told by the sea cadet authorities that this will be one of the best camp locations in all Canada.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that they are closing down that camp near Comox? If so, can he give us any idea of how much money has been spent in putting that camp there? They put extensive buildings there last year and the year before, and it is a thoroughly equipped camp. After all that expense, what is the idea of shutting it down?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

speechtext: The sea cadets.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What is Whitecliff camp used for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As a sea cadet camp during the coming summer.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Might I ask on whose recommendation that is to be used, and who owns it now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As I said, I have no particular reason for giving this information, because the matter does not come under my jurisdiction in any way. I have nothing to do with the provision of camps for sea cadets. That is done by the Navy League of Canada mainly, and while I do not know this definitely, I assume that the British Columbia branch of the Navy League are the people who arranged for this site.
I believe the hon. member for Yale also asked how much of our wireless equipment was made in Canada. As far as we can estimate up to date, Canada supplied 47-6 per cent; the United States, 33-2 per cent, and the United Kingdom, 19-2 per cent.
The hon. member for Cumberland asked about the cost of repairs to ships. I told him it would take some time to get the individual cost of each ship or of any particular ship, and that it would be very difficult to separate repairs from alterations and additions, which, strictly speaking, are not repairs at all but which are usually carried on at the same time as repairs. The total cost of repairing corvettes during the year was $3,984,000; that is an average of roughly $50,000 per ship. The average cost of repairs, alterations and additions to destroyers was in the neighbourhood of $170,000 per ship. The cost for minesweepers was about $25,000 per ship.
The Jion. member for Camrose asked about office machines. We estimate that for the present fiscal year the cost of all rentals of that kind will be about $10,500. That includes every type of office machine-duplicators, adding machines and so on.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I asked the minister last night in connection wtih the barracks at Aldergrove; and I should1 like also to ask who recommended Whitecliff.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I
am telling my hon. friend that he knows as much about that as I do.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Well, I know nothing about it. I went out of my way to get information about the sea cadets, but I do not select camps for the sea cadets, nor do I pay for the construction of camps. We cooperate with the Navy League of Canada, which has general supervision over sea cadets, to this extent, that we send some officers there to supervise the training. But we have nothing whatever to do with selecting

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the site, building the camp, or paying for it. That is done by the Navy League and I should assume that in this case it was dealt with, by the British Columbia branch of the league.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I asked a question yesterday in connection with the barracks at Aldergrove. First of all, may I thank the minister for his revelation. I should like him to give me a reply to my question of yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The matter about which the hon. member for Fraser Valley inquired may be answered in this way:	There are two stations in the locality,
one a receiving station and the other a sending station. I do not know a great deal about the technical side of this, but I am informed that the stations have to be some distance apart for technical reasons. Consequently in this case they are some fifteen miles apart. Both stations will be completed shortly. The permanent accommodation for the personnel is being provided at one station only, which will take care of about fifty persons, two officers and a little over forty men, but it will be all at one place. The men who go from one station to the other will be transported by panel truck and they will be returned to their barracks at night.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It will be a permanent barracks?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know that it will be permanent, but it will be good for the war at any rate.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: In the course of my remarks on the minister's estimates I endeavoured to focus his attention on the position of medical doctors in the merchant navy. Has the minister done any thinking about that? While he correctly points out that his department has no jurisdiction over the merchant marine, that it comes under the Department of Transport, yet the port medical examining officers of the merchant navy are called up. The Department of Transport has no power to call up men; therefore some defence department institutes the call in the first instance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Not the navy. I may tell my hon. friend that we do not call anybody up. It must be selective service.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is pretty much the one organization.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The naval examining board has the say as to who is accepted. Selective service is merely one of the cogs in the machine.
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City). Oh,no.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What I am trying to do is to point out the injustice that is done to the medical officer who is obliged to accept a position-and it is a very important one-in one of our ports across Canada, without the right to wear a uniform, with a great differential in income, without any assignment of pay to his family. Many of these men are of military age and desire transfer to one of the other branches of the service; but they are denied that right. I am wondering what the attitude of the department is with respect to correcting what I consider to be a great injustice to that particular classification. I mentioned it a few days ago. The minister in the course of his remarks pointed out, and, as I said, correctly, that his department had no jurisdiction over the merchant marine. I think someone should accept responsibility for that situation. These men are doing a very important job. They are on call at all hours of the night. This particular matter more properly belongs to the naval department. It is a job that requires a qualified medical practitioner. He is requisitioned for service. I think he should have all of the rights and privileges that go to those in the service, because he has no choice as to what he shall do.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question? Is he sure that those doctors are called up by some department of government and compulsorily assigned to these posts? I do not know of any doctors being called up in this country up to the present. There may be, but I thought the medical doctors had an association or branch called the medical procurement and assignment board that looked after all that, looked after the rights of all doctors. It is lather a surprise to hear that doctors have been called up under some compulsory arrangement and made to serve at ports, as my hon. friend describes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not any more sure of the mechanics than the minister is. I am mentioning the possibilities and I think the minister should know. .

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Why should I? I have nothing whatever to do with the doctors. I am not the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Pensions and National Health or the Minister of Labour. I am trying to run one department. I am not trying to run five or six. I have no more to do with that than I have to do with the call-up of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Every port in Canada is under the jurisdiction of the navy to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Not in that respect.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: A naval commander is in charge of each port. I consider and will hold responsible the Department of National Defence for Naval Services for any matter that occurs in or around those ports.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order. I believe the minister has answered the question.
