speechtext: I believe it is out of order to discuss this question under item 13. I believe it is the duty of the hon. member to speak on the item now under discussion. The minister has given an answer to the questions that come within the confines of his department.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: A few minutes ago the minister undertook to change the order of business in order to answer questions that had been asked previously. The question I am now discussing is one that I asked on a previous occasion. I want an answer to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Will my hon. friend state his question then?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My question was stated clearly. I wish to know the attitude of the Department of National Defence for Naval Services with respect to correcting what I consider to be a great injustice to medical men serving as examining officers at the different ports across Canada. These men are classified as serving with the merchant marine.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What is the injustice?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They are obliged to serve without uniform and without the regular pay and allowances that men in the naval services receive. They are not granted the right of transfer. The minister asked me if I knew what the mechanics were. I know this much about it. I discussed the matter with one doctor, a man of about thirty-five years of age. He tried in every way he could to transfer to one of the other services and was not able to do so. That man would not be in that position voluntarily. I assume that the medical procurement board must have assigned him to that position.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend is stating a totally different proposition now. He began by indicating that this was my responsibility. I suspect that my hon. friend has not the facts of his case correctly. I am not talking about the mechanics or anything of that sort. I am asking if he is sure that certain medical doctors in this country are taken by some government department and

placed in a position in which they do not want to serve. If they are, this is the first I have ever heard of it and I do not think it is so. I do not think my hon. friend has the facts. This man may be employed by the Department of Transport or by the immigration branch or by the Department of Pensions and National Health; I do not know. There is no compulsion about those departments, as I understand it; none at all.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: My argument is that these doctors should be given the same rights as the medical doctors in the navy. If the Department of Pensions and National Health is employing them I am very much surprised.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am sorry to intervene in this argument. We have several doctors in the various ports of Canada who are employed mostly for the inspection of sick personnel on ships that come into the harbours. We have tenders, launches. We go out and inspect the ship and we provide hospitalization for the personnel on the ship through our doctors. There is no compulsion whatsoever, so far as I am aware.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: These men are civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I should like to ask another question. To the minister's knowledge has any of the cost in connection with Whitecliff been charged the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I know nothing of any cost. I did not know of the name Whitecliff until I received a memorandum a few moments ago saying that this was to be the site of that camp. So far as I know there is no cost to this department or this government.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I have been looking through the list as we have gone along, to see if I could get the figures in regard to the cost of maintaining the Wrens; that is, the women's auxiliary of the naval force. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

War Appropriation-Naval Services
for example, the cost of food for the Wrens and the cost of food for the male personnel would come under one item, but I could make a fairly accurate shot at it. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: At some future time would the minister give us some estimate of the cost of establishing and maintaining the Wrens to date?

speechtext:
Then perhaps the
minister will take this as notice of the question.

speechtext: Would the minister tell me under what item I can get some information in connection with what I think are called baby carriers; I am very much interested in those.

carriers were taken to the west coast of Canada, where certain alterations were made in them. That was done for the British navy, not for the Canadian, navy.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am still wondering about the personnel to whom I referred a moment ago. Could the minister explain why these men are not entitled to dependents' allowance for their wives?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: They are Canadian nationals attached to the Royal Navy, but according to a letter I have received they are not given the Royal Navy marriage allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If I had the letter I would be glad to look into the matter, though if they were Canadians who joined the Royal Navy directly, without going through the Canadian navy, they would be out of my control and I would have no record of them. If my hon. friend would send me the letter I should be glad to look into the matter and try to get the information for him either from our own service or from some of the British naval officers here in Ottawa.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I have had it up with the British people, but I did not get much satisfaction.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The other
evening, when the minister's estimates were before the committee, I asked what progress was being made in the experiments with the Russian dandelion, from which the Russians are apparently extracting synthetic rubber with some degree of success. I notice, from page 20 of the minister's report, that some experimentation has been going on. Would he care to avail himself of this opportunity to tell, first of all, what progress has been made, and second, what plans his department has for a more extensive use of this Russian dandelion, with a view to using it for the production of synthetic rubber?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
As I said the other night, the
experiments being carried on in connection with dandelions are being carried on at the experimental farms. I would ask the hon. member to withhold his questions until we reach the experimental farm vote, which is only two or three down the list.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Except that the minister, himself, discussed it in his report for the year ended March 31, 1943. At page 20 the minister devotes almost a whole page to a discussion of the different developments respecting a substitute for rubber, and one for kapok.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The only thing I can say is that my hon. friend apparently has read the report, and he has read all I can give him about it. I have in my hand some material which I can read, if it is thought desirable.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Is it not true that these dandelions are being raised on farms, in addition *o the experimental farms?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I understand they are not; in any event, any information we have with regard to them is gained from the growing of them on the experimental farms. If there is any seed out anywhere it will be as a result of the farm activities. I can give that information much better when we get to the item for experimental farms.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I had in mind what appears in the minister's report, and I thought he might be able to tell us the result of the experiments carried on under this item respecting botany and plant pathology. The hon. member for Mackenzie points out to me that the report ends March 31, 1943, almost a year ago. I would imagine that the department would have gained some further information, first as to the percentage of latex they are getting from this dandelion plant-if I remember correctly the Russian scientists found they were getting about twenty per cent latex. What success have we had with those experiments? Second, does the government plan to make seed available in any large quantities to farmers, or to set up any facilities for the use of latex, when produced for the manufacture of finished rubber products?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The research in this
connection is continuing at the present time. Returns obtained are all the way from three per cent to ten per cent. But the experiments have not gone sufficiently far for us to be able to give final information with regard to it. Again I say that this matter can be discussed much more readily and to much better satisfaction when I have before me the officials who are directing those experiments on the farms. Some of the work, naturally, is being done by research people, and some is being done by our own chemists, in connection with examinations into the results from certain plants. But the experimental work is being done on the experimental farms, and when the time comes to distribute the seed they will be the agencies which will make that distribution, just as they make it in connection with wheat, and every other product.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: If the minister prefers to leave it to the experimental farm item, I shall have no objection, except that we would not want to be shut off when we reach that item.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: No, the discussion will not be shut off. We shall discuss it fully.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Will the minister, under the item for plant pathology, make a statement about the research carried on by his chemists and plant pathologists with regard

Supply-Agriculture
to flax rust. The minister will remember that last year, particularly in Saskatchewan, almost all varieties of flax, with the exception of royal flax, were badly affected with rust. The royal variety seemed to be more rust-resistant than vhe others. A good many thousands of acres of flax were almost competely destroyed1 by the rust. I believe it is the first time in my experience in Canada that I have ever seen flax rust. I remember the minister saying last year that some experiments were being carried on with a view to dealing with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I am sorry to have to
say again that that is experimental farm work, and that it is being carried1 on there. There was considerable rust on flax last year; that is, in 1942. In 1943 I do not think the rust did the same damage. Of course the reason for the difference in the amount of rust lies in the type of season. There was more moisture in 1942 than in 1943, and the more moisture there is, the more rust of all kinds will be found. But again, I could discuss this item to better advantage when the experimental farm item is before the committee.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I understand that experiments have been carried on in connection with finding a substitute for kapok. What success has there been in that connection? At the same time he might tell the committee what success we have had in Canada with regard to raising medicinal plants, such as digitalis, belladonna and henbane? What has the department been able to do in connection with supplying Canada with medicinal plants of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The only information
we have, in addition to what appears in the report which, I would judge, hon. members have been reading, is a statement to the effect that, in connection with kapok, in 1942 large quantities of milkweed floss and cat-tail floss were collected for tests being carried out in a search for a substitute for kapok, in cooperation with the national research council and the Royal Canadian Navy. It was shown that floss has a high value for the purpose for which it is being used.
With regard to the other matter in connection with medicinal plants, the division provides information on medicinal and related plants from! many sources from coast to coast. On account of a war-time shortage of drugs and the closing-off of some sources of supply, attention has been given to possible production in Canada. Experimental work has been initiated to provide necessary information. Close contacts have been maintained with the ministries of agriculture and health in the
United Kingdom, the Departments of Trade and Commerce and1 Pensions and National Health, the medicinal plants committee of British Columbia, and manufacturing chemists. Considerable quantites of digitalis, belladonna and1 henbane have been grown to increase the available seed supplies. Most of that work is being carried on in British Columbia.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Has the minister the
figures as to the actual supply obtained in 1943?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: No; we have no figures with regard to that. It is practically all being carried on in cooperation with the department of agriculture of British Columbia.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: During the last two years there has been a considerable increase in this item. Last year there was an increase of $25,938 and this year there is an increase of $15,581, approximately $45,000 for the two years. Such an increase requires an explanation and I should like to have it from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The total increase is $15,581, and of this $15,015 is for increases in temporary pay. The cost of living bonus and other items amount to $4,493. Miscellaneous items amount to $293. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Is that for extra temporary help taken on or increases in pay for the present temporary staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Part of it is for extra help taken on and part is to cover statutory increases in pay.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: What type of work is the minister contemplating to warrant an increase of $15,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
It should be remembered that in connection with the civil service the term "temporary" is not used in the sense one would expect it to be. For example, in Saskatchewan, where I had some experience, a person went on the temporary list for six months. If he were kept on for six months, he became permanent. In the dominion service a person may be temporary for twenty years, or even fifty years as my colleague suggests. These temporary people may have been on the staff for a considerable length of time and they get their increases as we go along. Much of this increase is to covei increases in pay of a very considerable staff which has been on from year to year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: There have been no notable results as yet that would be of any use to any one. Studies are being carried on in connection with the campaign against the sawfly, but as yet nothing has been discovered that will help us.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I am not going to complain about the minister spending too much; I am going to complain about his not spending enough. When we consider what has been done over a period of years by these branches, the small vote being asked for is really quite insignificant. The discovery of rust resistant wheat has meant millions of dollars to the farmers of this country; yet the salaries being paid to some of the scientists at work in our laboratories reflects no credit upon the department or the country. When the minister's estimates were before us the other night I complained about two veterinaries who were receiving $2,520 a year each. The minister stated that they had been with the department for fifteen or twenty years. These men had a college training which cost nearly as much as the training required by a medical doctor.
I have a list taken from the public accounts of the personnel in this botany and plant pathology branch who are receiving over
[Mr. Gardiner.}
$2,400. There are forty-three in the list, but only two receive more than $4,000 a year. Sixteen receive over $3,000, but the great number run $2,400, $2,700, $2,800, and so on. I see the names of some of my classmates in university twenty years ago. These were among the brightest and most promising students in the university. Many of them went to the United States to take postgraduate courses and had a remarkable sense of loyalty when they returned to this country to start in at a salary of $2,000 a year. Now, after nearly twenty years of service some of these men receive salaries below $3,000.
It has been suggested that under a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation government there would be regimentation and no rewards for private initiative. Some of the brighest students in the university of Saskatchewan have turned down offers from private industry and are now working for $2,400 a year. Many of them would have been receiving $10,000 had they remained in the United States. It is not good enough for the Minister of Agriculture to say that because farm products have been selling at low prices the people who are doing research work should be poorly paid. If that is a sound principle, then I suggest that we carry it out in regard to the minister himself. If, when butter is selling at ten cents a pound and eggs at three cents a dozen, the Minister of Agriculture is paid in butter and eggs, then I think we shall quickly have some adjustment in the machinery that determines what returns should come to our farming people.
These scientific people are paid either too much or too little, and in my opinion it is too little. If they had been paid more I feel sure that there would have been better morale among the large staff of the Department of Agriculture and we would have had better leadership from this department during the times when everyone was facing such a difficult situation. Could the minister give the committee any information as to the possibility of these people in his department who are in the $2,400 salary range being able to look forward to getting enough to permit them to own homes in Ottawa or to be able to rent suitable quarters? The cost of living in the capital city of the country is very high, and I do not see how the department can hold at these salaries honour graduates and those who have taken post-graduate courses in United States universities. What are the prospects of having the salaries increased and having promotions made to higher positions?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
On the general question as to why our expenditures are as low as they are in the different branches. I call attention

Supply-Agriculture
to the fact that in 1940 the appropriations were $13,000,000 for ordinary expenditures in this department. That had decreased to $9,000,000 in 1941 and to $8,887,000 in 1942, and in 1943 the figure was $8,996,000. The only reason for the decreased appropriations is the fact that we are at war, and after we had entered the war our expenditures were reduced. In 1940 the expenditure was, in round figures, $11,800,000; in 1941, $8,500,000; in 1942, $8,400,000, and in 1943, $8,492,000. The figure in the estimates this year for ordinary expenditure is $9,296,000, which is a little higher than it has been for the last two years. As I have said, the only reason for the expenditure being down is the fact that we are at war, and we have not yet got back to the level that prevailed before the war. But if you go back a few more years to the time when I first became Minister of Agriculture in 1935 or 1936, you will find that the estimates were not quite as high then as they are now. They amounted then to between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000; I have not the exact figures before me. We were successful in having the appropriations on ordinary account increased, so that in 1940 they stood at $13,000,000, but since that time we have cut them down because of the war, and I imagine that they will not be greatly increased before the end of the war.
So far as the salaries are concerned, I think every minister in the government believes that his staff is underpaid and from time to time he puts forth an argument in favour of increasing the pay of certain members of his staff. That always results in an examination being made into the salaries paid for comparable positions in other departments. The civil service commission examines into the salaries and classifies the employees of the different departments, and when a man accepts a certain position in the Department of Agriculture or any other department, it does not matter what his university or other qualifications may be, he is paid the salary attached to that particular position. He accepts a position in the civil service in preference to entering the realm of private competition or doing some other work, and he is paid the salary that pertains to his position. The positions are filled as a result of persons making application for vacancies that are advertised by the civil service commission in the press and at post offices throughout the country.
As I said the other night, every employee in a particular branch is a veterinary, and while it is true that two of them are receiving $2,400 a year, others are receiving between $4,000 and $5,000 a year. So that just the fact that they are veterinaries does not explain the whole
thing. It is the particular job the individual is doing that fixes his compensation. I do not know that there is anything more I can add. We all would like to see pay increases for the staff, but that would mean collecting more taxes with which to pay the higher salaries. If salaries throughout the whole civil service were increased, they would naturally be increased in the Department of Agriculture.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The minister has had a number of men and women working on the wheat rust problem for a period of years. Would he give the committee the names of those who have been working on rusGresistant wheat and the salaries we are paying them, and state how long we are to have to wait before the employees receive more reasonable compensation?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The list of those persons will be found partly under botany and partly under experimental farms, but from the list we have here I could not state who are working full time and who are working only part-time on rust, because many individuals are working on different problems as well as rust. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Do these employees receive superannuation, and, if so, how large a pension would they receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The Civil Service Superannuation Act is much the same as the Saskatchewan act with which my hon. friend is familiar. As a matter of fact, when I put through.the act in the Saskatchewan legislature it was based on the principles of the federal act so far as pension payments are concerned. The pension is based on the number of years of service, up to a maximum of thirty-five years service. Alter ten years of service the civil servant who is retired is paid one-fiftieth of his average salary for each year of service he has put in. If, for instance, he had put in thirty-five years of service he cojild draw thirty-five-fiftieths of his salary. Contributions are made by salary deductions from the employee's monthly salary, and an equal amount is contributed by the federal treasury into the superannuation fund.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Do the temporary employees also come under the superannuation act?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The temporary employees do not come under the superannuation act, but on retirement a payment is made to them which is I think, roughly one month's pay for each year of service.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: So that an employee who had been working for twenty-four years would receive two years salary as a retiring allowance? Is that it?

speechtext: The hon. member for Mackenzie asked a question with respect to certain rust-resisting grain. As I understand it, that would come under the item for experimental farms.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Before the minister gets away from the question of superannuation, would he tell the committee at what age the farmer gets his superannuation, and what the amount is? I ask this because I do not believe there is anyone in Canada who works harder or longer hours.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The hon. member, being a "fair" farmer himself, can give us that information, I think, better than anyone else.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: That is a very important question which was raised by the hon. member for Battle River-where does the farmer come in as regards superannuation? I should like to tell the hon. member that if he would put aside the price of a package of cigarettes every day from the time he was twenty-one years of age and apply it to the purchase of a government annuity such as we enjoy to-day by virtue of the social legislation brought dojvn by a Liberal government in 1908, he could have superannuation at the rate of $100 a month at the age of sixty-five.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Have you tried it?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: That is a Canadian government annuity. And that is my answer to a farmer or any other person who-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Have you tried it?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Will the hon. member let me finish? The question which has been raised is rather important, although it is probably out

of order as far as the agriculture estimates are concerned, but why not settle it? We are always asking for new legislation to provide new privileges and new ways of doing things. Why not use the things we already have? We have that annuity system, and it has been on the statute books for twenty-five years. speechtext: Before getting away from this question-

speechtext: This is the seventeenth of old Ireland, and I should like to have just one more word. I want to advise the hon. gentleman that I do not smoke; also, that the easiest way to get rid of some of the mentality we have in connection with the farmers is to clear the dead-wood out of their organizations.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Brant has supplied us with all the answers except, that to where the farmer is to get money to buy a package of cigarettes every day.
I wish to support the plea of the hon. member for Mackenzie. It seems to me that the whole picture with reference to agriculture is changing very rapidly.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: It has changed.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
In Great
Britain, the United States, andi the Soviet Union there seem to have been tremendous changes going on, envisaging new uses for agricultural products, interesting farmers in new methods of production, and1 bringing forward scientific methods which were not dreamed of even a few years ago. Part of the reason for the advancement made along these lines is the painstaking work which has been carried on by scientists, not only agricultural research workers but scientists in other fields. I believe the minister is sympathetic to the point of view we are now expressing, and may I say to him that I believe the committee would support him if he came here and pointed out that in the period following the war there will have to be tremendous readjustment in agriculture, and that that readjustment can be made only

Supply-Agriculture
if there are well-trained scientists andi if there is scientific data available to the farmer to begin to meet the post-war problems which will face Canada as one of the great agricultural exporting countries of the world. I feel certain that the minister would get the support of the committee if he would ask for a larger appropriation so as to make it possible not only to pay these scientists well but to get the necessary equipment to set up other laboratories for further research into scientific agriculture.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Under this item, I
believe, is carried on the dominion government weed survey. Could the minister tell us whether or not the following weeds are on the increase or decrease in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta: sow-thistle, Canadian thistle, wild- oats, pigweed and mustard seed?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
We have not the data
as to the general increase or decrease of the weeds mentioned. I can only tell the hon. member that wild oats are decreasing on my farm, that French weed is increasing, and that we did not have any sow-thistle ten years ago but the wind has blown a little in, and we see the occasional one. One could go over the whole province in that way and perhaps, if he examined all the different farms, come to a conclusion whether this or that weed is increasing or decreasing.
Generally speaking, the older the area becomes, the more weeds are to be found there. I think weeds generally have been on- the increase in western Canada ever since I wen-t there, forty-two years ago. At that time you could scarcely find weeds in wheat. Now you can find almost any weed you like to look for without travelling very far in western Canada.
One thing, probably, is not very well understood-. There are insects that sometimes combat weeds. The grasshopper, for example, did a very good job in certain parts of Manitoba a few years ago in destroying sow-thistle, and farmers who live on the Portage la Prairie plains area tell me that you could- go out in the fields and see grasshoppers standing on their heads sucking the last drop of juice out of the roots of the sow-thistle. So that what we call pests, and are pests in one direction, help us in another. That, I think, is true all through the vegetable field. Sometimes we get help where we least expect it. One of the reasons why my farm has less wild oats on it to-day than it had at one time is that-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
You have been too
busy to sow wild oats.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Yes, they were sown
before I got there. But there is a particular grub known as the cutworm, which cleans wild oats out of a field- more completely than I have ever been able to do with my summerfallowing.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: In connection with the weed seeds, is it true that a tolerance of three per cent, or thereabouts, of weed seeds was allowed in feed grain shipped from the prairie provinces to eastern Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
There was a tolerance of one per cent until last fall. It wras then found impossible to get grain for feed moved here under that regulation. That was a regulation entered into as a result of cooperation between the provincial governments in the east and the federal government; but last fall the provinces and the federal authorities got together and agreed that a tolerance of three per cent would be allowed in order to permit of grain coming by Fort William without having to be unloaded and cleaned. Labour could not be secured with which to unload and clean the grain sufficiently fast to move it. That slowed up the loading and unloading of cars, and therefore in order to take care of the feed situation here the grain was allowed to come down with a seed allowance of anything up to three per cent. Up to that amount it was allowed to go by. Of course that was widely advertised at the time. The farmers were warned that the grain was coming down with a possible three per cent of weed seeds

in it. They were warned that they should examine this grain and either have it cleaned in the east or clean it themselves after it arrived.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The minister mentioned the shipping of grain to the east and the provincial departments of agriculture. I should like to know how his department and the provincial departments work in so far as weed control is concerned. In that connection I do not want the hon. members from eastern Canada to think that we raise a great deal of weedy crops out west. We raise a considerable amount of grain comparatively free from weeds. As the hon. minister pointed out, as time goes on and land gets older there is an increase in weeds. By different tillage operations, different methods of cultivating, it is possible to combat the weeds to a great extent. In the west we have different climatic conditions in certain years. Those conditions may sometimes cause a farmer to have a weedy crop in a certain year on land that he thought he had fairly well cleaned out of weeds in the preceding years of cultivation. Because of that I wish to warn the minister that while he may think his land is freer from wild oats now than it was in earlier years it is possible that in another year he may be surprised to find that there is a decided increase in wild oats. He may think he had not sowed any, but the wild oats may grow from seed sowed years ago. I have known wild oats to lie in the ground for seven years, land that had been sowed down to grass. When it was ploughed it was found that there were still wild oats there that had not been destroyed during that length of time. On the whole, whenever the farmers in the west have an opportunity to farm their land under favourable weather conditions they try to produce grain with as few weeds as possible. I should like to know how the provincial departments of agriculture work in with the Department of Agriculture here?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Of course we do study ways and means of controlling weeds through (he work at our experimental farms and in other ways. As the hon. member for Humboldt knows, the actual control of weeds or the putting down of weeds is under the provincial authorities, and usually they have legislation which calls upon the municipal authorities to assist in the keeping down of weeds. That is done in both eastern and western provinces. There is cooperation in the studying of ways and means of controlling weeds. Sometimes what is looked upon as a weed in one area is looked upon as a useful plant in others, because of the use that is'made of it. All that

Supply-Agriculture
work is carried on in a cooperative way between the two jurisdictions. Most of the control work on the ground is done provincially or municipally.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: May I follow up that statement? The Department of Agriculture here acts in an advisory capacity to the other departments in assisting experiments?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: An endeavour is made to prevent overlapping in the work?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

speechtext: I should like to ask another question with respect to the tolerance of three per cent of weed seed in feed grain shipped to the eastern provinces. Did I understand that this has the approval of the minister's department and the approval of the departments of agriculture in the eastern provinces where this feed grain is shipped?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Yes; it was all discussed with them at the time. As a matter of fact, we received a lot of criticism at the time because we did not act until we received the permission of the eastern provinces to act.
' We did not take action until they were consulted. I might say that all this discussion on weed seed really comes under the item of plant products farther down. This item has to do with pathology, the study of diseases, really.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: While the control of weeds may be largely under the provincial governments, nevertheless would the minister not say that the operation of the wheat acreage reduction measure had brought about an appreciable reduction of weeds in some areas? Would the minister give some information as to the results that have been obtained in that direction during the past year's operation of the wheat acreage reduction? Inspectors are going around inspecting the land. Have they not noticed whether there has been a better control of weeds?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I wigh members of the committee would allow me to discuss this matter when we get to that item; otherwise I shall have to discuss it half a dozen times. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: But weed surveys are made under this item, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Yes, weed surveys of a kind are made under this item. That question was all right, and I answered it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The men in the department who are carrying on experiments in connection with the killing of weeds may be doing a good job, but no matter what the department does, the great part of this killing of weeds has to be done by the farmer himself. The minister says that weeds are more prevalent in certain districts. In the district south of the Qu'Appelle valley, just opposite the minister's own farm, in the early days the stink-weed was a blessing in disguise, because the farmers had to get down to real farming to kill it and there is hardly any of it there now. On the other hand, we are being cursed with certain other weeds, though we will handle them in due course. We had a lot of sowthistle; we have mastered that. We had some mustard; we have pretty well mastered that. In some districts, however, certain weeds are allowed to grow in order to overcome the effects of dry weather, and in our country we are now getting Russian thistle. What has been the experience of the department in controlling that weed? In the Wood Mountain district they allow that plant to grow in order to control the dry weather, and in the winter they leave it on the land. In the spring it rolls, and now it is rolling up into our country, where it is becoming a curse with us because we do not need it for the same purpose. Could the minister give us a little information in regard to the control of the Russian thistle?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the Russian thistle was really imported in to this continent. I understand it was brought here from Russia, or at least from some place on the continent of Europe, and planted by someone in the northern United States, I think in Montana or one of the neighbouring states. It is a plant that grows in dry seasons; it is more or less liked by animals if they are short of other feed, and mixed with straw it makes a fodder on which live stock can get by in difficult seasons. Whoever brought in the thistle certainly brought it to an area where it would spread, because it rolls; and in the prairie country, where there is nothing to stop tumbling mustard or a weed of this kind it rolls over the country, seeding itself as it rolls, so that it spreads very rapidly. This plant really was not known in western Canada twenty or twenty-five years ago, but now it covers practically the whole west. It changes the appearance of the prairie country in a dry season; it becomes a sort of a brown colour, which is not at all inviting, but the plant itself is perhaps helpful in a dry year, when nothing

Supply-Agriculture

else is growing. My experience is that it grows very little in a year when you have plenty of moisture; you just see a very small plant at the bottom of the crop, enough to reseed for another year. I assume those who brought it in did so for that very reason, and I do not know that a great deal of effort has been made to control it up to date, even by farmers cultivating the land. They make use of it when the season is such as to make that necessary; they stack it and feed it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: There is no doubt that the Russian thistle came to the United States first, and from there it spread into the southern part of western Canada which I have the honour to represent. Russian thistle grows very thickly in dry weather; it prevents soil drifting and is very helpful in that respect. In wet weather it does not grow to any size at all. It does not interfere with crops; it is not injurious in any way, and we rather favour it because it helps in dry weather and can be used to a certain extent for feed.

The report we have on grasshoppers in 1943 is this. Grasshoppers were relatively of little importance on the Canadian prairies in 1943. In Manitoba the insects were present in such small numbers that provincial authorities made no provision for the setting up of mixing stations or the preparation and distribution of poison bait. It will be understood by all hon. members, particularly those from the west, that the provincial governments carry on the campaign against grasshoppers. In Saskatchewan baiting was carried out on an extremely restricted scale, and only in two or three localized areas where grasshoppers were abundant. Mixing

Supply-Agriculture
stations were operated in certain areas of Alberta, but the amount of bait used was abnormally small. The grasshopper population has been diminishing on the prairies for a number of years, this condition having been brought about by natural causes, chiefly the weather.
Services carried out in 1943 indicated that although there might be a slight increase in certain sections, these insects are not expected to be of great importance during 1944.
In British Columbia the situation is entirely different. A serious outbreak occurred in the range country, and in some parts of the province grasshoppers were more abundant in 1943 than has been the case for many years. Not only were range grasses destroyed over extensive areas, but gardens were invaded and vegetable crops severely damaged. Services indicate that grasshoppers will be present . in large numbers again in 1944. This is a general report for the western provinces.

We do assist in making surveys, in order that they may know that this movement of grasshoppers is on the way. It starts in the United States, as a rule, in the state of Minnesota, then across to Manitoba, then into Saskatchewan. The next year they will be in Alberta. It has passed over those

provinces, and this year it is in British Columbia. We make the surveys because, first, it is international, and, second, it is interprovincial. But the matter of fighting grasshoppers is done by the provinces, assisted by the municipalities. They are right on the ground where the fighting is to be done. The provinces have been following the practice of accumulating poisons, and having storage space for those poisons in the areas where infestations are threatened. Then the poison is spread by the farmer, himself, about the fields where his crops are. As a rule it is spread by ploughing a furrow around the field, putting the poison in the furrow; then the grasshoppers are presumed to hop into that furrow, eat some of that poison-and they do not hop out again. Then they may destroy some of the crop in a strip roundabout; poison is spread there, and when they eat the poison they are destroyed. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe referred to forests and forest products, when another item was under discussion, and I believe the minister told him to bring it up again under the item for entomology. The hon. member is conversant with our forests, and in regard to the budworm infestation I feel the same as he does. I understand that this year about 40,000 square miles are affected. Our forest products are very important to our internal and external trade, and particularly to our tourist trade. In fact agriculture in Canada could not exist if it were not for our forests. The accessible forests of Canada have been destroyed ten per cent during the past six or seven years.
This budworm, or bud-caterpillar, does considerable damage. It really is a caterpillar which eats the buds and destroys the tree. After it is dry, it is very susceptible to forest fires. Could not the dominion government get together with the provinces to work out some scheme to protect our forests? In cutting a fire-break a province can carry it only to its border when it must quit. Unless the other province continues on from that point, part of the work may be wasted. The dominion government should step in to supervise the cutting of fire-breaks and to see that they are kept clean. Proper watersheds should be provided. There was an article in the press of March 13, to the effect that the budworm infested balsam and fir principally, and if fir and balsam ran over forty per cent in an area, the budworm became very prevalent. This work would have to be carried out in cooperation not only with the provincial governments but with the United States because they are having the same trouble with the

Supply-Agriculture
budworm. Can the minister tell us what his department is doing on this? I know it is quite a problem, but it means life or death to the tourist trade and also to the lumber trade of Canada, because I have seen districts where hundreds of acres have been absolutely dried out by this worm.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The position in relation to battling the budworm is much the same as in relation to battling grasshoppers. We do the research and make surveys and give out advice to those who have the responsibility of caring for the resources of their province. The fact that there is an international aspect to the surveys and to the information given out makes it necessary that that particular end of the work should be done by this department. I have in my hand a memorandum on spruce budworm outbreaks which I think will give the committee full information.
The present spruce budworm outbreak in Ontario covers a very large area of forest lands, including some forty-five thousand square miles. About 18,000,000 cords of balsam fir and white spruce have been killed or injured beyond hope of recovery. There is no artificial method of control for a forest insect outbreak of this kind that can be applied over such a great area of forest lands. Aeroplane dusting with poisoned dusts was studied carefully by this department during the former spruce budworm outbreak some twenty years ago. The technique of application was perfected, but with the insecticides available at that time only partial control of the spruce budworm could be obtained, although other defoliating forest insects were readily destroyed. New and more effective insecticides are now available, and tests with them will be carried out next summer in Ontario forests. The application of insecticides from aeroplanes may eventually be utilized for the control of defoliating forest insects on areas of specially valuable timber, but the high cost of the operation will prevent its use over very large areas of pulpwood lands.
During the former spruce budworm outbreak, forest entomologists of this department made an intensive study of all methods of controlling the insect that seemed possible of application, and their report clearly stated that, although an outbreak by the spruce budworm extending over enormous areas could not be controlled by artificial means, it should be possible so to manage a pulpwood forest that in the future spruce budworm outbreaks would not develop therein. The recommendation in brief was that pulpwood lands should be managed so that over-mature stands of balsam fir would be utilized as rapidly as possible, and the balsam fir cut thereafter on a short rotation,
leaving only rapidly growing stands on the ground, and also that the reproduction of spruce and mixed stands should be encouraged by every practicable means.
That recommendation still stands, and it is maintained by our entomologists that, if destructive outbreaks of this insect are to be avoided in the pulpwood forests of eastern Canada in the future, extensive areas of overmature balsam fir must not be permitted to accumulate. Intensive studies of the present outbreak are in progress, and our forest entomologists are prepared to assist the companies in carrying out recommendations for salvage, control, and prevention, whenever and wherever such assistance may be required.
Unfortunately, economic conditions were such that the recommendations of our entomologists were not followed in our pulpwood forests, and the present outbreak in northwestern Ontario is duplicating the former great outbreak that spread through Quebec and the maritime provinces. There is now some evidence that the operators of large areas of our pulpwood forests are becoming interested in the recommendations of the entomologists and have expressed their willingness to cooperate. It is to be hoped that management plans along the lines that are recommended will soon be put into operation. A definite effort is being made to join forces with the United States forest authorities in studying this problem, and an international committee of experts has been organized for this purpose.
The problem of appropriate forest management for the prevention of future outbreaks has many ramifications extending into fields of activity other than that of forest entomology, such as forestry and industrial chemistry. Limitations imposed by war-time conditions are unavoidable in the execution of a full programme of action. This situation can be dealt with more completely in our plans for post-war rehabilitation, but preliminary management plans should be prepared and applied without delay on several large areas in territory as yet unaffected by the present outbreak. In other words, preventive activities ought to be carried on in areas that are not yet infested.

speechtext: Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre)': On Monday we shall take up first of all the resolution on the war appropriation and the estimates of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and we may call two items in, order of supply during the day. If we do call them, they are on the Department of the Secretary of State and civil estimates of munitions and supply. Possibly we may have to discuss further the civil estimates of agriculture, and the house must be prepared to take into consideration at any time Mr. Speaker's report on standing orders.
May I ask what the minister means by saying that we might have to discuss two further items of munitions and supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is the intention to call two new items.
Apart from that, we are going into committee on war appropriations and take up munitions and supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Monday, March 20, 1944
